### p9
*2026-08-16 12:37*

> continue

Deploy landed. Let me verify the live state and check one thing about that commit.

**Build 186 is live — the shim works, and it's a 6× speedup on every device where the GPU says yes.** Your phone is the remaining question mark, and it'll answer it by itself the next time you record a note.

**What the experiment found.** I made ort's device request visible for the first time: it unconditionally demands `timestamp-query`, `shader-f16`, `subgroups`, ten storage buffers per shader stage, and 4GB buffers — never once asking the adapter whether it has them. WebKit grants several of those only partially, and a single refusal slams the whole door. That's the iOS failure, precisely located.

**What failed, on evidence.** Handing ort a pre-acquired device through its documented `executionProviders: [{name: 'webgpu', device}]` API builds a session fine, then dies on every inference with `Failed to wait for the operation:3` — the bundle's future-wait machinery only tracks devices its own instance created. I tried three descriptor variants (default, clamped-limits-only, features-only); all three died identically. So the door is the descriptor, not the device — which is what pointed at the fix.

**What worked.** A small taming module wraps `GPUAdapter.requestDevice` with haze's exactly-what's-offered recipe: requested features intersect with the adapter's, max-limits clamp down, alignment limits clamp up, unknown limits drop. On desktop Chrome the clamp changes nothing (the adapter offers everything) and the numbers came out **223ms warm versus 1.4s on wasm** — about 6×, with byte-identical transcripts.

**The stranded-iPhone scenario, proven end to end.** I set a fresh profile to the exact state your phone is in — pinned to `wasm` by the old fallback — and ran the real engine: the pin was retired, the audition passed, WebGPU engaged, warm run 225ms, no re-pin. That's one automatic retry per install; if your phone's GPU still declines, whisper's kernels fail at runtime and `/phone`'s existing fresh-module wasm fallback catches them exactly as before, re-pinning so it never nags again. No new failure modes, and nothing to operate.

**A hygiene item paid for itself.** The toggle proof initially passed dishonestly — `tame.js` lingered in `site/` after unticking, which is exactly notes.md hygiene item #9 ("stale asset trees", predicted 2026-08-15). fmlink now keeps an asset manifest per build and sweeps files it placed whose owner has left the composition; only linker-placed files are ever deleted. Re-running the toggle then gave the honest answer: swept, 404, pin honoured, wasm path intact. Item #9 is ticked with the caveat that pre-manifest strays need one tick/untick cycle to clear.

Two small notes: the commit swept in a one-line whitespace tidy you made to fm.md — harmless, but it's your file so you should know it rode along. And the desktop result proves *no regression*, not victory; the simulator is useless here (it exposes `navigator.gpu` with a null adapter), so the real iPhone is the only judge.

**In my lane — can whisper itself stream?** Three findings, and they point the same way:

The reference implementation, [whisper_streaming](https://github.com/ufal/whisper_streaming) (the IJCNLP-AACL 2023 [paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.14743)), gets **3.3 seconds** of latency on long-form speech using a LocalAgreement-2 policy — it commits a token prefix once two consecutive updates agree on it. That's server hardware and quality-optimised settings, so it's the pessimistic end.

The lever we'd gain by owning the runtime is real: whisper.cpp's `audio_ctx` parameter shows [roughly 3× speedup](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp/issues/1855) on short clips by shrinking the encoder's 1500-frame context to fit the actual audio. That's exactly what the exported ONNX graph can't do and our own kernels can. The catch is honest and documented: the decoder was trained on 30-second windows and "starts to glitch" when you deviate too far, so it's a lever with a quality cost that has to be measured rather than assumed.

The most encouraging find is a 2026 paper, [WhisperPipe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25611), reporting **89ms median end-to-end latency** (142ms at p90) within 2% of offline Whisper's accuracy — and critically, **it doesn't modify the model at all**. It's pure inference strategy: hybrid VAD (Silero plus an energy gate, cutting false activations 34%), dynamic buffering with overlapping context windows, and adaptive scheduling. That matters strategically, because it means the streaming architecture is a layer *we* build regardless of which model sits underneath. The model choice and the streaming design are separable.

For the VAD component we'd also have to hand-write, [Silero VAD](https://github.com/snakers4/silero-vad) looks well-suited: 309K parameters, ~1.2MB, **MIT licensed**, STFT plus a small encoder and RNN, operating on 32ms chunks. An energy gate with a pre-roll buffer is the trivial v1 if we want to defer the RNN kernels.

**Still running:** one agent surveying streaming-native alternatives (Moonshine, Parakeet/FastConformer, Kyutai, Zipformer, transducers) with licensing and architectural complexity weighted for hand-written WGSL, and another on what's actually proven for WebGPU inference in mobile Safari — buffer limits, f16 availability, achievable matmul throughput, and AudioWorklet capture quirks. I'll synthesise all three into a revised `sovereign.md` once they land.

**One question only you can answer**, and it shapes the architecture more than anything else: what latency class do the functions you have in mind need? Live captions that update *while* you speak (sub-second, continuous, expensive) are a very different build from push-to-talk dictation with live feedback, which is different again from command recognition where the answer lands a moment after you stop talking — and that last class is where WhisperPipe's 89ms figure actually lives, since VAD-segmented latency is measured from end-of-utterance. If you tell me which of those the functions need, I can size the design honestly instead of building for the hardest case by default.

> # In-browser ASR with WebGPU on iOS — research report (16 Aug 2026)
> 
> ## Source-quality warning up front
> 
> A large fraction of 2026 search results on this topic are AI-generated SEO pages (byteiota, webo360solutions, ayoob.ai, testmuai, explainx, johal.in, digitalstrategyforce, brandlens). They recycle the same handful of numbers, several of which are **wrong or badly out of date**. I've traced the important ones back to primary sources and flagged the bad ones explicitly below. Treat anything I haven't marked "verified" as a claim.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## 1. iOS Safari WebGPU status — the load-bearing facts
> 
> ### Verified
> - **WebGPU ships enabled by default on iOS 26 / iPadOS 26 / macOS Tahoe 26 / visionOS 26.** Apple's own words: *"WebGPU has been enabled in Safari Technology Preview for over a year, and is now shipping in Safari 26 beta for macOS, iOS, iPadOS, and visionOS."* ([WebKit blog](https://webkit.org/blog/16993/news-from-wwdc25-web-technology-coming-this-fall-in-safari-26-beta/), [gpuweb Implementation Status](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/wiki/Implementation-Status)). Compute shaders are explicitly included.
> - **caniuse timeline** ([caniuse.com/webgpu](https://caniuse.com/webgpu)): iOS Safari ≤17.3 unsupported, 17.4–18.7 present but **disabled by default** (WebKit feature flag), **26.0–26.5 supported**. So your PWA gets WebGPU only on iOS 26+, and only for users who've updated.
> - **`shader-f16` is supported and Apple actively recommends it on iOS.** From WWDC25 session 236, *"Unlock GPU computing with WebGPU"* ([video](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2025/236/)): *"On iOS and visionOS specifically, storing data in f16 or compressed formats can really help you avoid getting your program terminated due to memory pressure."* And: *"even if you just store the data in half precision and immediately unpack to f32, you'll still get a lot of memory benefit."* Enable via `requestDevice({requiredFeatures:['shader-f16']})` plus `enable f16;` in WGSL. (Note: WebKit bug [254668](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=254668) is still marked NEW — it's stale; the WGSL compiler was rewritten since. Trust the WWDC session and feature-detect at runtime.)
> - **Subgroups are NOT in shipping Safari yet.** They landed only in [Safari Technology Preview 249](https://webkit.org/blog/18182/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-249/) — the sole WebGPU line in those notes is *"Added support for subgroups in WebGPU."* (317145@main), roughly 3 weeks ago. Subgroup-matrix (the tensor-core-equivalent) is further out still; the Llamas-on-the-Web authors say subgroup matrix ops were *"not yet available in stable browser releases."*
> - Safari 26.2 added WebGPU-in-WebXR and direct `GPUTexture` as depth-stencil/resolve attachments ([WebKit 26.2 features](https://webkit.org/blog/17640/webkit-features-for-safari-26-2/)) — nothing compute-relevant.
> 
> ### Corrections to widely-repeated misinformation
> 
> **(a) The "256 MB on iPhone 6 → 993 MB on iPad Pro" buffer-limit table is from January 2021 and is not about WebGPU.** It originates in [gpuweb issue #1371](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/issues/1371), which reported `MTLDevice.maxBufferLength` on iOS 12/13 devices to argue for a spec limit. That issue is closed; the spec's baseline `maxBufferSize`/`maxStorageBufferBindingSize` defaults came out of it. The Medium article "WebGPU bugs are holding back the browser AI revolution" reprinted it as current Safari behaviour and every SEO site copied it from there. **Do not plan against those numbers.** Query `adapter.limits` on the actual device.
> 
> **(b) "WebGPU requires an iPhone 15 Pro or later"** — [MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/guide/ios-26-safari-features/) states this flatly. It contradicts Apple's own WWDC25 statement (*"WebGPU is supported on all platforms where Metal is supported, specifically: Mac, iPhone, iPad, and Vision Pro"*), the WebKit blog, and caniuse. **I could not verify it and believe it is wrong** (probably conflated with a hardware-ray-tracing or Apple-Intelligence requirement). Still: feature-detect `navigator.gpu` and have a path for its absence; you cannot afford to be wrong about this in either direction.
> 
> **(c) "Safari on iPhone does not support float32, only float16"** — from [transformers.js #973](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js/issues/973) (Oct 2024). This is almost certainly a misreading of **texture** capability: rendering-to and filtering-of 32-bit float *textures* is unsupported on iOS ([gpuweb #4417](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/issues/4417), `float32-filterable`). f32 arithmetic and f32 storage buffers are fine. **Irrelevant to you** — you'll use storage buffers, not textures.
> 
> ### Real iOS blockers (verified, and these are the ones that matter)
> 
> | Blocker | Evidence |
> |---|---|
> | **Safari per-tab memory cap &lt;500 MB on iOS.** This, not buffer-binding size, is the binding constraint. | [Llamas on the Web (arXiv 2605.20706)](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.20706v1): *"on iOS devices Safari tab memory is limited to &lt;500 MB."* Their iPhone 17 Pro Max could only fit the four smallest models tested. |
> | **f16 accumulation produces incoherent output on Apple GPUs.** They disabled it and accumulate in f32. | Same paper: *"f16 accumulation disabled on Apple M-series due to incoherent outputs (using f32 instead)."* |
> | **ONNX Runtime Web JSEP is catastrophically broken on WebKit 26** — CPU pinned at 400%+, memory to 14 GB+ after inference completes, survives `session.release()`, kills the WebProcess on iOS. Root cause traced to a loop in JSC's Wasm OMG compiler (`parseAndCompileOMG → prepareForGeneration → GraphColoringStackAllocator → HashTable::rehash`). Unresolved, no workaround. | [onnxruntime #26827](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/issues/26827) (macOS Safari 26.2, iOS 26 sim, ORT 1.20–1.23.2) |
> | **onnxruntime-web WebGPU has never officially supported iOS**, any browser. Open since Nov 2024. | [onnxruntime #22776](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/issues/22776) |
> | **Transformers.js leaks on Safari** — third-party measurement: *"memory usage of Transformers.js on Safari climbed to 10 GB until the tab was eventually killed."* | [arXiv 2605.20706](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.20706v1) |
> | **Unexplained device-lost in Safari 26 WebGPU** (macOS 26.1 + iOS 26) with an Emscripten/WASM WebGPU app; works in Chrome/Firefox/wgpu-native. No validation message emitted. Filed with Apple, unfixed. | [imgui #9103](https://github.com/ocornut/imgui/issues/9103) |
> | **WebContent + GPU process crashes on iPhone 15 / iOS 26.4**, stable on iPad same OS. Reproduced in Safari and Capacitor by a second reporter. Apple asked for Feedback Assistant filing; unresolved. | [Apple forums 822200](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/822200) |
> | **Cache API quota on iOS ≈50 MB**; model weights must go to **OPFS/IndexedDB** (multi-GB, but disk-fraction based). And **origin data is evicted after 7 days without user interaction** — a PWA that isn't opened for a week re-downloads its weights. | [WebKit storage policy](https://webkit.org/blog/14403/updates-to-storage-policy/); [transformers.js #1298](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js/issues/1298) shows `QuotaExceededError` killing whisper-web on iPhone |
> 
> **Bottom line for §2:** WebGPU-the-API is genuinely there on iOS 26 and compute works. The hard ceiling is **~500 MB of tab memory and a young, buggy Metal-backed implementation**, not shader capability. Every framework that tried to ship ML to iOS Safari in 2026 hit memory or process-death, not missing features.
>

> ## 2. What others have achieved
> 
> ### The two papers you should actually read
> 
> **[Llamas on the Web (arXiv 2605.20706)](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.20706v1)** — a WebGPU backend for llama.cpp, hand-written WGSL, benchmarked on **16 GPUs from 8 vendors including iPhone 17 Pro Max on Safari**. This is the single most relevant prior art for what you're doing.
> - Decode throughput Llama3.2-1B q4_k_m: 65–100+ tok/s high-end desktop, 30–60 mid-tier, **4–17 tok/s on the mobile/"low" cluster** (which includes the iPhone).
> - 54–69% better decode than WebLLM/Transformers.js; 29–33% lower memory.
> - Native comparison: **Metal native outperforms WebGPU by 1.5–2×**; CUDA by 2.5–10×. WebGPU safety/bounds checks alone cost **5–42%**.
> - Key engineering moves, all directly applicable: static allocation of *all* runtime memory at startup (no dynamic buffer creation); a single rotating **parameter-buffer arena** to replace push constants (WebGPU has none); streaming weights **OPFS → GPU buffer through four 1 MB staging buffers**, never materializing in the WASM heap. That last one is what let them serve larger models on Safari specifically.
> - They wrote their own WGSL preprocessor (`pre-wgsl`) because **WGSL has no preprocessor** — the same complaint Ratchet made.
> - Missing from WebGPU that they had to work around: **bf16, u16, u8, native 4-bit, push constants, buffer aliasing** (the last kills in-place ops).
> - Verdict, quoted: *"WebGPU provides functional portability but not performance portability."* An autotuning sweep over thousands of configs on 4 vendors gave **41% over hand-picked kernel parameters**.
> 
> **[Characterizing WebGPU Dispatch Overhead (arXiv 2604.02344)](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.02344v1)** — this is the paper that will save you the most time.
> - **Per-dispatch overhead: 24–36 µs on Vulkan, 32–71 µs on Metal.** Safari's Metal path measured **31.7 µs**, notably better than wgpu-native Metal at 71.1 µs.
> - Naive benchmarks *overestimate* dispatch cost by ~20×; they had to use sequential-dispatch measurement.
> - **At batch=1, per-operation overhead dominates regardless of kernel quality.** Cutting dispatches 876 → 564 bought **53% throughput**.
> - Fusion payoff is backend-dependent: RMSNorm fusion gave 1.4–1.7× on Vulkan but **nothing on Metal** (0.95× wgpu, 0.91× Safari). A tiled 3-dispatch approach vs unfused 7-dispatch gave **2.0× on Metal**, 1.17× on Vulkan.
> - Also the source of the "unoptimized WGSL matmul reaches only 1–2% of FP32 peak; ~17% achievable" figure.
> 
> **Implication for whisper-shaped work:** Whisper's decoder is autoregressive at batch=1 — exactly the regime where dispatch overhead dominates. A whisper-small decoder layer naively unfused is easily 30–50 dispatches/layer; at ~32 µs each on Metal that's ~0.5 ms/layer of *pure overhead* before any math. **Dispatch count is your primary design variable, ahead of kernel quality.** The encoder (one big batched pass over 30 s of mel) is the opposite regime and is compute-bound — optimize it as a real GEMM problem.
> 
> ### Projects
> 
> | Project | Status / relevance |
> |---|---|
> | **[whisper-turbo](https://github.com/FL33TW00D/whisper-turbo)** (Fleetwood) → became **[Ratchet](https://github.com/huggingface/ratchet)** | Rust + hand-written WGSL, WebGPU-only, first-class quantization, lazy eval, in-place ops. Closest architectural cousin to what you're building. [RFC: Ratchet V1](https://github.com/huggingface/ratchet/discussions/187) is worth reading for the honest post-mortem: *"WGSL has absolutely no preprocessor, which is extremely limiting compared to Metal"*, and *"with the current architecture, it's not possible to fuse even unary ops into their predecessors."* Notably, a transformers.js commenter pointed at whisper-turbo as *the* WebGPU Whisper that actually worked on iPhone and Android — but that predates iOS 26 and I could not verify it today. |
> | **[transformers.js](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js) + ORT Web WebGPU** | The mainstream path. Whisper works well on desktop; **broken or unsupported on iOS** (issues 973, 1298, ORT 22776, ORT 26827). Its docs still carry an Oct-2024 warning banner. |
> | **[whisper-web](https://github.com/xenova/whisper-web)** / [Real-time Whisper WebGPU](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Xenova/realtime-whisper-webgpu) | Reference demos. WebGPU is on an experimental branch. iOS reported broken (#1298, quota). |
> | **[Moonshine Web](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js-examples/tree/main/moonshine-web)** | Moonshine Base, real-time in-browser ASR, WebGPU with WASM fallback. Faster and more accurate than Whisper at equal size. No iOS claims. |
> | **[parakeet.js](https://github.com/ysdede/parakeet.js)** | NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6B in-browser. Interesting architecture: **encoder on WebGPU, decoder on WASM** — a pragmatic split that dodges exactly the batch=1 dispatch-overhead problem above. Has `createStreamingTranscriber()`. No published RTF, no Safari/iOS claim. |
> | **[ggml/llama.cpp WebGPU backend](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp)** | Exists (`ggml-webgpu.h`), WGSL shader library with pipeline wrappers, a **parameter arena** for batched dispatch (same trick as the paper), and subgroup-matmul paths where available. No published mobile numbers. |
> | **[wgpu-llm](https://github.com/Beledarian/wgpu-llm)** | Explicitly "no framework, raw WGSL shaders" Llama inference in Rust. Good reference for kernel-per-op structure, native-only. |
> | **[wonnx](https://github.com/webonnx/wonnx)** | 100% Rust WGSL ONNX runtime. Appears dormant — last meaningful activity traced to 2023. Its [`gemm.wgsl`](https://github.com/webonnx/wonnx/blob/master/wonnx/templates/matrix/gemm.wgsl) is still a useful read. |
> | **[WebLLM/MLC](https://github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm)** | M3 Max: Llama-3.1-8B-q4 ≈41 tok/s (~80% of native MLC); Phi-3.5-mini ≈71 tok/s. MLC already ships a **[fallback to 256 MB `maxBufferSize`](https://www.mail-archive.com/commits@tvm.apache.org/msg108799.html)** when 1 GB is refused, plus a 128 MB `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` fallback — motivated by iOS Safari and Android Chrome respectively. Copy this pattern. |
> | **[nnJIT (arXiv 2309.08978)](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.08978v2)** | JIT kernel autotuning for in-browser DL on edge devices. Avg **2.77× GPU (WebGPU)** kernel speedup, up to 8.2× model-level, by tuning tile sizes, unrolling, vectorization, workgroup config — search space pruned from millions to dozens. Evidence that runtime autotuning beats static kernels on mobile. |

> ## 3. WGSL matmul on Apple mobile GPUs
> 
> ### What's achievable
> - **[Optimizing a WebGPU Matmul Kernel for 1TFLOP+](https://www.nuss-and-bolts.com/p/optimizing-a-webgpu-matmul-kernel)** is the best step-by-step. On **M2 Pro (~6 TFLOP/s fp32 peak, 200 GB/s)**:
>   - naive 1-thread workgroups: **1.64 GFLOPS**
>   - `workgroup_size(256)`: ~200×
>   - 2D `workgroup_size(8,8)` + **swapping which dimension maps to row vs col** (cache-coalescing) — large win, easy to get backwards
>   - 4×4 per-thread tiles: marginal — *because the compiler wouldn't unroll variable-bound loops*
>   - **manual unrolling + 8×8 per-thread tiles: 3× over 4×4, crossing 1 TFLOP/s** ≈ **17% of peak**, ~1000× the naive kernel.
> - So: **~17% of fp32 peak is the realistic WGSL ceiling** without subgroups, corroborated independently by the dispatch-overhead paper. On an A18-class iPhone GPU (order ~2–4 TFLOP/s fp32) that puts you around **300–700 GFLOPS sustained** — a rough extrapolation, not a measurement. I found **no published WGSL matmul GFLOPS measured on an actual iPhone**; that's a genuine gap you'll have to fill yourself.
> 
> ### Apple-GPU-specific tuning constraints
> From Apple's Metal guidance ([Metal shader performance best practices](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/tech-talks/111373/), Apple dev forums [709208](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/709208), [780112](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/780112)):
> - **32 KB threadgroup memory per GPU core.** Allocating all 32 KB to one workgroup drops you to **one resident workgroup per core** — occupancy collapse. Budget ~8–16 KB so 2–4 workgroups stay resident. For an f32 double-buffered 64×64 tile you'd need 2×(64×64×4)×2 = 64 KB — **doesn't fit**. This is the single biggest reason to store tiles as **f16 in workgroup memory and accumulate in f32 registers**.
> - **SIMD width is 32** (`threadExecutionWidth` / `threads_per_simdgroup`). Make workgroup size a multiple of 32; 64/128/256 are the sane choices.
> - **Threadgroup shape matters at equal thread count** — 16×16 vs 32×8 differ measurably.
> - Coalescing: adjacent invocations must touch adjacent addresses.
> - Mobile-vendor sensitivity in general: Adreno can be **5–7× slower** with a bad workgroup size; Mali is nearly insensitive. Apple sits in between but is not insensitive.
> 
> ### Concrete recommendations for your kernels
> 1. **Autotune at startup.** Sweep {workgroup size, tile M/N/K, per-thread tile, vec width} over a few dozen candidates for ~1 s and cache the winner in localStorage keyed on the adapter string. This is nnJIT's finding (2.77×) and Llamas-on-the-Web's (41%) and it's cheap.
> 2. **Manually unroll.** Do not trust the WGSL→MSL compiler to unroll loops with non-constant bounds. Generate unrolled WGSL from a template — you'll need your own preprocessor anyway (WGSL has none; both Ratchet and LlamaWeb built one).
> 3. **`vec4&lt;f32&gt;` / `vec4&lt;f16&gt;` loads.** Not covered in the nuss-and-bolts post but standard practice; Metal wants wide loads.
> 4. **f16 storage, f32 accumulate.** Apple explicitly recommends f16 storage for memory pressure; the LlamaWeb team found **f16 accumulation gives incoherent results on Apple GPUs**. Do both.
> 5. **Don't design around subgroups yet.** Ship a portable path; add a `subgroups`-gated fast path later, feature-detected. Shipping Safari doesn't have them as of today.
> 6. **No push constants.** Use one rotating uniform "arena" buffer with dynamic offsets, reset per submit.
> 7. **No buffer aliasing** — plan for ping-pong buffers, not in-place ops.
> 8. **Minimize dispatches above all** at batch=1, and note that on Metal, *elementwise* fusion may buy you nothing — fuse at the tiled-GEMM level instead (the 3-dispatch-vs-7 result gave 2.0× on Metal).
> 9. **Bound each compute pass.** GPU watchdogs kill long-running work (Chrome ~2 s, Windows TDR 5 s; Metal has its own). Keep any single dispatch well under a second, especially for the encoder over 30 s of mel.
>

> 
> ## 4. Audio capture on iOS — this is where I'd expect you to lose the most time
> 
> ### Verified quirks
> - **AudioContext starts suspended.** Must be created or `.resume()`d **inside a real user-gesture handler**, not on load. Universally reported.
> - **Hardware sample rate is 48 kHz on iPhone 6s and later** and cannot be changed at the audio-unit level ([Apple forums 104550](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104550)). Requesting `sampleRate: 16000` in getUserMedia constraints has been reported to **silently produce no audio at all** on iOS Safari — no error thrown ([cognitive-services-speech-sdk-js #256](https://github.com/microsoft/cognitive-services-speech-sdk-js/issues/256)). **Capture at 48 kHz and resample 3:1 to 16 kHz yourself** (in the worklet or a worker). Do not fight the hardware rate.
> - **Starting the mic force-routes output to the speaker**, even with wired/BT headphones attached — a long-standing iOS Safari/Chrome behaviour. Causes howling feedback if you also play audio. Relevant if your PWA ever speaks back.
> - **AudioWorklet's fixed 128-frame render quantum** is a recognized pain point on mobile: [web-audio-api #2632](https://github.com/WebAudio/web-audio-api/issues/2632) — *"the mandated low 128 sample latency is causing massive distortion across all mobile devices and browsers."* Don't do heavy work in the worklet. Ring-buffer 128-frame blocks into a SharedArrayBuffer and let a worker do resampling/mel/VAD.
> - `ScriptProcessorNode` is deprecated and glitches under load — AudioWorklet is the only real option (available iOS 14.5+).
> - **SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation** (COOP/COEP headers). Plan your serving headers now; retrofitting is painful.
> 
> ### The background/lock-screen blocker (hard, no workaround)
> - **iOS suspends Web Audio and WebRTC the moment the screen locks or Safari backgrounds.** Multiple Apple developer forum threads: [774239](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/774239) (*"Safari Should Allow Background WebRTC for Real-Time Audio Apps"*), [689182](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/689182) (WKWebView `microphoneCaptureState` goes muted on backgrounding), [762582](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/762582) (PWA lock-screen audio dies after 30 s paused).
> - **There is no PWA workaround.** No background-audio entitlement is available to web content. If your product needs to keep transcribing with the phone in a pocket, **you need a native shell** (a Capacitor/WKWebView app with the `audio` background mode, or native capture feeding the webview). This is the single biggest product-level constraint in this whole report and it is worth deciding on early.
>

> 
> ## 5. Streaming ASR: architecture guidance
> 
> ### The model choice matters more than the kernels
> **[Moonshine v2 (arXiv 2602.12241)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12241)**, Kudlur/King/Wang/Warden, 12 Feb 2026 — this is purpose-built for exactly your problem and you should probably target it rather than Whisper.
> - Sizes: **Tiny 33.6M / Small 123.4M / Medium 244.9M** params.
> - Avg WER on Open ASR: **12.01% / 7.84% / 6.65%**. LibriSpeech-clean 2.08% (Medium).
> - Response latency on Apple M3: **Tiny 50 ms (5.8× faster than Whisper Tiny), Small 148 ms (13.1× vs Whisper Small), Medium 258 ms (43.7× vs Whisper Large-v3)**. Compute load 8–29%.
> - **Sliding-window self-attention gives bounded TTFT independent of utterance length** — Whisper's full-attention encoder makes TTFT grow linearly with prefix, which is the structural reason streaming Whisper is awkward.
> - Windows: first/last two layers (16 left, 4 right) frames; intermediate layers (16, 0) strictly causal. **50 Hz feature rate → 80 ms algorithmic lookahead, 320 ms left context.**
> - **No positional embeddings anywhere in the encoder** ("ergodic" — translation-invariant); position is injected only in the adapter before the decoder.
> - Encoder emits *provisional* states immediately, *finalized* states once right-context arrives.
> - Explicit target: **0.1–1 TOPS edge processors with sub-1 GB memory** — i.e. it was designed for your envelope.
> - Benchmarked on ONNX/CPU. **No browser or WebGPU deployment published** — that's the gap you'd be filling.
> 
> **Why this is a big deal for a hand-written-kernel project:** the small/medium Moonshine v2 at f16 is ~250–500 MB *before* quantization, or ~60–130 MB at int8/q4 — comfortably inside Safari's ~500 MB tab budget, unlike Whisper-small. No positional embeddings and fixed local windows mean **fixed-shape kernels**, no KV-cache-length-dependent recompiles, no giant attention matrices. Sliding-window attention with a 16+4 window is a *tiny* fixed-size attention kernel. This is dramatically less WGSL to write than full Whisper.
> 
> ### Latency reference points
> - **Whisper-Streaming** ([ACL 2023 IJCNLP demo](https://aclanthology.org/2023.ijcnlp-demo.3.pdf)): LocalAgreement policy with self-adaptive latency, **3.3 s latency** on unsegmented long-form speech. That's the ceiling for chunked-Whisper approaches.
> - Standard browser chunking buffers 2–5 s → inherently ~2–5 s latency. **Silero VAD gating** to run inference only on speech segments is the standard improvement.
> - Moonshine v2's 80 ms algorithmic lookahead + ~50–260 ms compute is **an order of magnitude better** and is the only published approach that gets browser-plausible conversational latency.
> 
> ### Suggested architecture
> ```
> getUserMedia (48 kHz, echoCancellation/noiseSuppression on)
>   → AudioWorklet: 128-frame blocks → SharedArrayBuffer ring buffer (no DSP here)
>   → Worker: 48→16 kHz resample, log-mel (WASM or a small WGSL kernel), VAD
>   → WebGPU: streaming encoder, fixed-shape sliding-window kernels
>   → decoder: consider WASM/CPU at batch=1 (parakeet.js does exactly this)
>        — at 32 µs/dispatch on Metal, a small autoregressive decoder may
>          genuinely be faster on CPU than on the GPU
>   → main thread: provisional text + finalized text
> ```
> Weights in **OPFS**, streamed to GPU buffers through small (~1 MB) staging buffers, never materialized in the heap. Never Cache API (50 MB cap on iOS).
> 
> ---
> 
> ## 6. Priority list for someone hand-writing WGSL for iPhone ASR
> 
> 1. **Measure the actual device first.** Ship a one-page probe: `navigator.gpu` present, full `adapter.limits` dump, `adapter.features` (`shader-f16`, `subgroups`, `timestamp-query`), and a 3-line matmul microbenchmark. Do this on your real target iPhones **before writing kernels**. Every number in the public record about iPhone WebGPU limits is either from 2021 Metal or from an AI-written blog. You will be the primary source.
> 2. **Budget against ~500 MB of tab memory**, not against buffer-binding limits. That's the verified killer.
> 3. **Pick Moonshine v2 (or a Moonshine-shaped local-attention encoder) over Whisper.** Bounded TTFT, fixed shapes, 6× smaller for equal accuracy, designed for exactly this envelope. Whisper's full-attention encoder fights you at every step.
> 4. **Count dispatches obsessively.** ~32 µs each on Safari/Metal. At batch=1 this dominates everything. Consider CPU/WASM for the autoregressive decoder.
> 5. **f16 storage + f32 accumulate.** Apple recommends the first; the LlamaWeb team proved the second is necessary on Apple GPUs.
> 6. **Keep workgroup memory ≤16 KB** (32 KB/core budget) and workgroup size a multiple of 32. Autotune the rest at startup and cache.
> 7. **Write your own WGSL preprocessor and manually unroll.** Both prior hand-written-WGSL projects (Ratchet, LlamaWeb) independently concluded this is mandatory.
> 8. **No push constants, no buffer aliasing, no bf16/u8/u16.** Design around all four now.
> 9. **Decide about background audio now.** Locked-screen / backgrounded capture is impossible in a pure PWA on iOS with no workaround. If the product needs it, you need a native shell.
> 10. **Have a fallback.** Given the state of Safari's WebGPU backend (two independent unresolved process-crash reports, one unexplained device-lost), wire up `device.lost` handling and a WASM path from day one. Note that **iOS Safari's Web Speech API can do on-device recognition** with an installed language pack ([`available({processLocally:true})`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SpeechRecognition/available_static), [`install()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SpeechRecognition/install_static)) — worth keeping as an emergency fallback, though it's reported **not to work in installed web apps on iOS**, only in Safari proper ([whatpwacando.today](https://whatpwacando.today/speech-recognition/)).
> 
> ### Biggest unknowns I could not resolve
> - No published WGSL matmul GFLOPS on any iPhone. My ~300–700 GFLOPS estimate is extrapolation from M2 Pro.
> - No published end-to-end ASR latency for any model on iOS Safari WebGPU. Nobody has demonstrated this working well; the frameworks that tried all hit memory or crashes.
> - Whether Safari's Metal backend enforces a compute-pass watchdog, and at what duration.
> - The MacRumors "iPhone 15 Pro or later" claim — unverified, contradicted by three better sources, but worth a five-minute test on an older device.

Toggle proven — unticked, the bug returns exactly. Re-ticking and shipping the fix:

**Picker fixed and shipped (build 190).** Root cause was a DOM loan: `/tucked-updates` moved `/policy`'s actual element inside `#changes`, and `/chooser` rebuilds that box on *every* panel open — so the second open deleted the picker outright, permanently until reload. The first research report is in, and it substantially changes the plan. Let me record the findings before they're lost.

**Two things landed: your picker is fixed, and the research has moved the plan considerably.**

**The picker (build 190).** It was a DOM loan gone wrong. `/tucked-updates` moved `/policy`'s actual element into `#changes`, and `/chooser` rebuilds that box on *every* panel open — so the second open deleted the picker outright, and `place()`'s careful `if (!seg) return` guard made the loss silent and permanent until reload. It now parks on the panel (hidden) across the rebuild and gets re-homed after; proven across four consecutive opens, and unticking the fix reproduces the bug exactly. My first attempt failed instructively, too: I parked it in a *detached* node, which `getElementById` can't see — so the parent couldn't find it either. The rule this establishes is in the spec: borrowing another feature's element is a loan, and the borrower owns both ends of it.

**On your use case — this is the most important thing I learned today.** Ambient conversation → semantic search → bullets changes the engineering in your favour, because **retrieval tolerates error but not latency**. A wrong word barely moves an embedding — "rhodes" still finds road facts — so we can spend accuracy on speed in ways dictation never could. And the retrieval half already exists: `/semantic-find` embeds and scores on-device with our own WGSL kernel today. What's missing is streaming ASR feeding it, which is one rung, not two systems.

**The model probably shouldn't be whisper.** Whisper's full-attention encoder makes time-to-first-token grow with prefix length — that's the structural reason streaming whisper is awkward, and why chunked approaches land at ~3.3s. [Moonshine v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12241) (February 2026) is purpose-built for exactly our envelope: sliding-window attention giving bounded TTFT, **no positional embeddings in the encoder at all**, 80ms algorithmic lookahead, and encoder states emitted provisional-then-finalized. Tiny is 33.6M params, 50ms response latency on an M3 — 5.8× faster than Whisper Tiny. For a hand-written-kernel project the structural wins matter even more than the numbers: fixed shapes, no KV-length-dependent recompiles, and a *tiny* fixed attention kernel instead of a 1500×1500 one. Nobody has published a browser/WebGPU deployment, which would make it ours to do.

**Three platform facts that reshape the design.** The real ceiling on iPhone is **~500MB of Safari tab memory**, not buffer limits — and the widely-quoted "256MB on iPhone" table everyone cites turns out to be from a 2021 Metal issue, not current WebGPU. **Dispatch overhead is ~32µs on Safari/Metal**, and at batch=1 that dominates everything regardless of kernel quality, which makes dispatch count our primary design variable rather than kernel tuning. And **WGSL has no preprocessor** — both prior hand-written-WGSL projects independently built their own, which means our feature-modular WGSL rung isn't a luxury, it's the thing everyone else discovered they needed.

Vindication on the sovereign turn, incidentally: onnxruntime-web's WebGPU has **never officially supported iOS**, and its JSEP path pins CPU at 400% and leaks to 14GB on WebKit 26 until the process dies. We were never going to win that fight.

**One decision I can't make for you.** iOS suspends Web Audio the instant the screen locks or Safari backgrounds, and there is **no PWA workaround** — no background-audio entitlement exists for web content. Ambient listening with the phone in a pocket requires a native shell. For canvassing, the phone is presumably in hand with the bullets on screen, so foreground-only may be entirely fine — but it changes what miso *is*, so it's worth deciding deliberately rather than discovering at rung 11.

All of this is now in `sovereign.md` §11 as a sourced research log. The second agent — surveying streaming-native models on licensing and architectural complexity for hand-written WGSL — is still running; when it lands I'll do the full revision of §§5–9, since the model section was written from memory and priors and now needs replacing wholesale.

The expanded report adds one genuinely important reframing. Let me fold it in.

**Both research reports are in, and the plan is rewritten. `sovereign.md` now targets Moonshine v2, not whisper.**

**The model.** [Moonshine v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12241) (February 2026), **MIT licensed**, English-only, safetensors weights. The tiny variant is 44.1M params, 88MB at fp16, and beats whisper-tiny.en on *both* accuracy (12.01 vs 12.81 average WER) and speed (50ms vs 289ms response latency on an M3). But the structural wins matter more to us than the numbers, because we hand-write every kernel:

It needs about **ten kernels** — matmul, layernorm, softmax, erf-GELU, SiLU, causal conv1d, asinh/exp, CMVN reduce, partial RoPE, embedding gather, argmax. What's *absent* is the real prize: **no FFT, no mel filterbank**, no transducer joiner, no LSTM, no beam search, no WFST decoder. Moonshine takes **raw audio** through a convolutional stem, which deletes an entire rung from the ladder along with the whole class of window/hop/filterbank mismatches that silently poison a frontend. Sliding-window attention gives bounded time-to-first-token — a 16-left/4-right window is a *tiny fixed-size* attention kernel rather than a 1500×1500 one — and there are no positional embeddings in the encoder at all. Fixed shapes throughout, so no pipeline recompiles.

**The most encouraging finding is a reframing of the risk.** Every documented iOS WebGPU failure in the public record — ORT's buffer pooling, JSEP's Wasm glue looping in WebKit's hash table, transformers.js leaking GPU memory to 14GB — is a **resource-management bug in a general-purpose runtime, not a hardware or WebKit compute limitation**. The worst pathology explicitly spares the plain WASM backend, which localises it to the JSEP layer. A runtime with explicitly owned, pre-allocated, reused buffers plausibly sidesteps the entire class. So I've promoted static allocation from a performance tactic to **L0's governing correctness rule**: every buffer created once at startup, reused forever, nothing allocated per inference.

That said, there's a report of a [crash after ~500 inferences](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/issues/27584) on iOS Safari WebGPU with no published root cause. A streaming loop hits 500 passes in about four minutes, so this is existential for rung 10 — which is why **rung 1 is now a probe**: dump the real device limits from your iPhone, run a matmul microbenchmark, and soak-test 10,000 dispatches. Find out on day one, not at rung ten.

**Three kernel constraints, now double-sourced.** Use `shader-f16` throughout (100% availability on iOS, and Apple's own stated defence against memory-pressure termination) but **accumulate in f32** — f16 accumulation produces incoherent output on Apple GPUs. Write every reduction with workgroup shared memory, never subgroup intrinsics (**0.02% availability on iOS** — the ~100% figure everyone quotes is macOS). And no single buffer over 256MB, which tiny at 88MB clears trivially.

**Both of the agents' remaining "unresolved, load-bearing" questions are actually answered.** Whether `navigator.gpu` exists in an installed standalone PWA — yes, proven by your phone's own failed run today. Whether capture survives backgrounding — no, and there's no PWA workaround, which is decision #2 waiting for you.

**Six rulings sit in §11.** The two that matter most: **foreground-only or a native shell** (ambient listening with the screen locked is impossible in a pure PWA — fine if the phone's in hand with bullets on screen, expensive to discover at rung 11), and **tiny or small to start** — tiny looks right given that retrieval tolerates error, but you know what a doorstep in Sevenoaks sounds like and the benchmark doesn't.

The ladder is thirteen rungs, and rung 11 is the actual product: *"the roads round here are terrible"* surfacing road facts on your phone, mid-conversation. Everything before it is scaffolding for that sentence.

**What was happening.** The healing was already occurring and then being *undone*. Your phone's boot order is: local metadata reseeds without transcript stamps → the scheduler queues a local attempt → `RecIndexed` arrives from the exchange and the good words are adopted → and then, half a second later, the local attempt fails and blanks them. The mirror was doing its job correctly; the failure raced it and won. This was the gap I recorded in `/mirrored-words`'s own spec this morning as a known accepted risk — "a slower local result can overwrite an equal-grade mirrored one" — which the field has now collected on.

**The rule the fix adds is narrow and absolute: an empty result may never replace a non-empty transcript.** A failed attempt reports a failure, not an erasure — silence is not information about what was said. The node compares the state before the event with the state after; when a failed `Transcribed` has blanked words that were there a moment ago, it puts back the text, rung and grade, and clears the error stamp with them, because the note isn't in a failed state — it simply wasn't *this* device that worked it out. Then it re-runs the scheduler, which finds the note already at the best reachable grade and stops asking. That last part is the second half of the healing: your phone stops retrying forever.

Proven four ways: good words survive a failure; an honest first failure with nothing to protect still reports its error (so we don't lose real diagnostics); a genuine later result still lands and replaces; and unticking the node reproduces the erasure exactly.

### p22
*2026-08-16 14:16*

> How come we’re hitting WASM memory limit? Transcription worked in the past

Good question — and the answer matters, because it points at something I broke. Let me check the evidence rather than speculate.

Found it, and it's my regression. Let me confirm the mechanism in the code before I explain.

**You're right to be suspicious — it's not a new memory limit, it's that we started loading everything twice. And that's my doing.**

**The arithmetic.** The model is much bigger than I'd assumed: the merged decoder is **82.7MB** and the encoder 8.6MB, so ~91MB of ONNX per load. Add the runtime: the WebGPU (jsep) wasm binary is 24.9MB, the plain one 12.3MB.

When the engine tries WebGPU and falls back, it does this:

1. **WebGPU attempt** — loads the jsep runtime (24.9MB), fetches the model into memory (~91MB), then fails at session creation with the missing `webgpuInit`.
2. **Fallback** — and look at line 103: `build('wasm', 'wasm-fallback')` re-imports transformers with a cache-busting query. That's deliberate (it's the escape from v4's memoized-failure trap I documented in `/phone`), but it means a **completely fresh module graph**: a second ort runtime, a second session, and the ~91MB model read in again.

So a single failed transcription now peaks somewhere around **200MB+** of buffers, versus ~104MB before. Against Safari's ~500MB per-tab ceiling, with the app, the page, and the audio blobs also resident, that's a plausible kill — and the exact peak depends on when the first buffer gets collected, which JS gives no guarantees about.

**Why it worked before.** The device was **pinned to `wasm`**. `pickDevice()` returned the pin immediately, so exactly one runtime and one copy of the model ever loaded. That's the configuration that ran happily for days. **`/tamed-request` retired that pin** — deliberately, that was its whole job — so now every attempt walks the expensive path first.

**Why it can't recover on its own**, which is the worse half. Look at where the pin gets written: *inside* the success path, after `run()` returns. If the wasm retry also fails, nothing is written. So the next attempt has no pin, probes again, double-loads again, and dies again — forever. And my tame's one-audition marker doesn't help, because there's no pin left for it to protect.

That means `/tamed-request` does not keep its own stated promise. Its spec says "a failed audition re-pins and is never repeated"; it relies on engine.js pinning on fallback success, which is precisely the case that doesn't happen when the fallback also fails. The node is wrong against its own words, and it's mine.

**One honest gap in the diagnosis:** I still can't tell you whether that OOM was your phone or your laptop — that receipt predates build 193, which added device identity. The next failure will say so outright.

**The fix I'd propose** (not shipped — you asked a question, not for a change): a small subfeature of `/tamed-request` that records the verdict of a failed audition. If a run fails with a WebGPU error, pin `wasm` immediately, regardless of what the retry did — we learned something real and should write it down. Every subsequent attempt then loads one runtime and one model, which is the shape that worked for weeks. It's falsifiable, too: the receipts will show `device: "wasm"` and a real transcript, or they won't.

Worth noting it's a bridge, not a destination — Moonshine at 88MB in fp16 replaces all 91MB of this, with one runtime we wrote, and no fallback ladder at all.

**Why now is exactly right by your own doctrine.** `/engine-receipts` was built this afternoon as one feature's private telemetry, and its spec explicitly names the general form as "deliberately not built". This is the second ask for the same mechanism, so **the promotion rule fires**: the parameter earns its variable, and receipts become a thin user of the general thing rather than a special case.

**Four parts, three of which are already in the tree.**

The **call site** should carry no bookkeeping: just `log(...)` in Rust and in JS fragments, with **the linker injecting the node path** — exactly as it already injects node paths for the context manager's tick gates. Nobody hand-writes a path, so nothing drifts when a node gets regrouped.

The **switch** is the context manager wearing a different hat: a user-scoped `feature_log` var mapping node path → level, with the same prefix semantics ticks already use. > Just wanna check: logging should still work when disconnected from the server - should go into local store for eventual upload or cleanup - as part of blackbox

Good check — let me verify rather than assume, because the interaction with the blackbox's bounds is where this could quietly go wrong.

Reading it closely, your requirement is met — but I found two things worth showing you rather than asserting. Let me measure.

Confirmed: one log line per event halves the flight recorder's memory. Two more checks — replay safety and genuine offline retention:

Verified — and the answer is yes on your requirement, but I found two defects I introduced, both latent because logging is off by default.

**Offline behaviour works as you want.** Measured directly: with the upload forced to fail, the lines stay in `log.entries`, the `sentT` watermark does *not* advance, and they're present in localStorage. When the network returns, the next flush ships them and the watermark moves. That's genuine store-and-forward, and it inherits the blackbox's four upload triggers — every 10s while visible, on the `online` event, on page-hide with a keepalive request, and at load, which is how a crashed session ships its tail.

**Defect one: logging doesn't honour replay's pause.** `/blackbox` sets `paused` during `/replay` so re-enactment isn't recorded as new history. My `emit()` pushes straight into `log.entries` without checking it. Measured: while paused, event deltas recorded 0 — correct — but log lines recorded 1. So replaying with logging on would pollute the record it's replaying from. One-line fix, matching what `record()` already does.

**Defect two, the more serious one: logging evicts the flight recorder.** The ring is capped at 500 entries *shared* between event deltas and log lines. I burst 400 events with logging on and the ring held **250 event deltas instead of 500** — logging halved the blackbox's memory with just one line per event. A feature logging ten lines per event would leave room for about 45 events. That's precisely backwards: switching on logging to investigate something would blind the recorder that explains it.

The fix I'd propose is a separate ring — `log.lines` alongside `log.entries`, with its own cap, shipped in the same batch and sharing the same watermark. Logging then can't crowd out events, and the two bounds can differ sensibly, since log lines are chatty and cheap while event deltas are precious.

**One property worth knowing rather than fixing:** `trim()` drops entries older than five minutes *whether or not they've been sent*. That's deliberate for the blackbox — it guarantees the retained window is always replayable — but it means "eventual upload" is bounded at five minutes of disconnection, after which it becomes the cleanup you mentioned. If you want logs to survive a longer outage, the separate ring could bound by count only and keep unsent lines until they're delivered. Also worth noting: `save()` swallows a localStorage quota error silently, so a full store means logging quietly stops persisting rather than complaining.

Both fixes are small and I'd do them as one subfeature of `/logging` — say the word.

Geography checks out across six continents, and mid-ocean correctly falls back. Toggle proof and ship:

Shipped as build 205 — and the toggle sweep removed the vendored asset too, so unticking leaves nothing behind. Now recording your principle:

**Build 205: the map button is now the country you're standing in.** And your principle is recorded — I think it's the sharpest idea of the day.

**The ask, shipped.** Once miso has a fix, the 🗺 becomes the outline of the country it falls inside, and it remembers between visits so it's right before you've taken a fix — you're almost always still in the country you were in yesterday. Verified across six continents: Paris → France, New York → United States, Tokyo → Japan, Sydney → Australia, Nairobi → Kenya, mid-Atlantic → nothing, which correctly falls back to the emoji.

**This is the vendoring rung `/map` named an hour ago, arriving because an ask needed it.** `tools/fetch_countries.py` pulls Natural Earth's public-domain boundaries at a pinned commit and reduces them to what an icon and a point-in-country test actually need — 175 countries in 147KB, served from our own origin, so no geocoding service is ever asked where you're standing. Gitignored like the speech and embedding assets: the recipe is the record.

One cost I've stated plainly in the spec rather than buried: simplification drops points closer than about 5km, so **within a few kilometres of a border the answer may be the neighbour**. Fine for a button; not fine for anything that depended on it, which is why it's written down.

State carries the two-letter code, never the drawing — an outline in loop state would be kilobytes copied into every blackbox entry for a picture the device can redraw for free. And the fill is `currentColor`, so `/tools`' existing monochrome filter turns it into a silhouette without this node knowing anything about the toolbar's palette.

**On your principle — I think the move underneath it is genuinely new.** Every tick in miso today enables or disables something that *exists*. A suggested subfeature is a line for something that doesn't, and ticking it wouldn't switch anything on — **it would file an ask**. The builder proposes, you choose, and the flywheel starts without anyone typing a wish. That closes a real gap, because asks currently require you to think of the thing *and* find the words, which is the slowest part of the loop and the part that most needs the app's help.

Most of the surface already exists: the chooser renders tickable feature lines, and `/review` already prepends a section of not-yet-yours features to that same list. "Suggested" is a third section in the same idiom — though a promise and a fact must never look alike.

The best part is where the suggestions come from. Every node I shipped today ends with named limits — `/map` names panning, antimeridian wrapping and offline vendoring; `/country-icon` names the border imprecision; `/logging` names the levels it deferred. Right now that's prose no asker will ever see. Carrying it into the tree export would make "anticipate subfeatures and consider how you'd build them" a documented obligation of writing a node rather than a private habit — paid once, by the person best placed to pay it.

I've left four open questions in the note: whether ticking files immediately or batches, whether suggestions expire, whether a node may suggest against another's subtree, and whether a shipped suggestion keeps its line or reappears as an ordinary row.

Both strip labels and keep buildings. Dark matches miso's shell, so that's the pick — with contrast lifted in CSS. First the parent refactor to make the tile source an extension point:

Now the node that swaps in the label-free style:

Tile route serves the quiet style and caches under its own name. The headless geolocation denial overrode the fix again — re-injecting:

All correct — 25/25 tiles, the lift replacing the parent's dimming, and both credits. Toggle proof and ship:

The toggle test was inconclusive (the headless geolocation denial raced my injected fix again), so let me prove it properly at the composition level:

The mini has cached tiles from before the style-scoped path — meaning the map was used on a real device. Tidying those and checking the evidence:

**Build 207: the map draws places, not names.** And there's field evidence in the cache — 50 tiles fetched under the old style and 25 already under the new one, so you've been looking at it.

**What changed.** OSM's standard raster bakes labels into the image — street names, that parking symbol, shop pins — so they can't be filtered out afterwards. The fix is a different basemap, not a different treatment of the same one. It now uses CARTO's `dark_nolabels`, built from the same OpenStreetMap data with every label and point of interest omitted.

**I checked the candidates by eye rather than trusting the name**, which mattered: the first tile I compared looked empty in every style, because it's a residential junction with nothing on it. On a dense tile over Soho the difference was clear — buildings and streets both survive the no-labels styles. A style that had dropped buildings would have satisfied your words and missed your point, since the proposal asked for buildings specifically.

Dark rather than light because miso is a dark app and a white rectangle would sit on the page like a hole. That basemap is drawn for dark pages, so `/map`'s slight dimming would have buried it; this node replaces the filter with a lift instead — enough to tell a building from the ground without turning the map into a lightbox.

**The parent gained an extension point rather than a special case.** `/map` now names the three things a tile style actually is — where the cache keeps it, where it comes from, and who must be credited — and derives its own behaviour from them. This node redefines all three together. Because the style name is part of the cache path, tiles of two styles can never be confused, and switching styles needs no cache clearing; the 50 orphaned tiles from the old layout were simply unreachable, and I've swept them from both machines.

Toggle proven at the composition level, which is more convincing than the DOM test here: unticked, there's no CARTO URL and no `quiet` style anywhere in the composed server; ticked, the linker's dispatcher resolves `tile_url` and `tile_style` to `feature_QuietTiles`, so the override demonstrably wins the chain. Attribution follows the toggle too — both parties credited with it on, OpenStreetMap alone with it off, which is then the truth again.

**One limit I've named in the spec**, in the spirit of your suggested-subfeatures principle: a map with no names at all is harder to talk about — *"meet me at the corner of…"* has nothing to read. If names are wanted back selectively, that's labels at high zoom only, or our own labels drawn from data we hold, and it's a different node.
